utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Usher, have the accused brought in, please. (Accused brought in)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Is everybody ready? Are our interpreter friends ready? Good day. Does the Prosecutor hear me? Does the Defence hear? General Blaskic, do you hear as well? After long discussions regarding the timetables, and trying to take into account technical necessities, the transcripts and also thinking about the fact that these are busy afternoons, generally speaking, and I repeat generally speaking, if we begin at 2.15, we will be finished at 6.45, with a 30-minute break, because apparently that is required, and this is also for technical reasons. This is the first point. Under special occasions, for reasons which might be related to appointments or to complete the testimony of a witness for whom the judges have some questions to ask, we would then finish within that time period in any case. Third, the Registrar is supposed to count the time that we have been using, especially if we are only meeting in the afternoon, or in the morning, that we spend about four hours doing so, and he will keep a very careful account of it, that is Mr. Dubuisson will, so that we can apply fully the order of 17th December which set a number of days for the Prosecution and a specific number of days for the Defence. I wanted to give you these clarifications. Of course telling you that, there can be some modifications having to do with the needs of the Trial Chamber or of the Prosecution, the Defence or the accused. We will decide things on a case by case basis. Having said that, I can give the floor to Mr. Cayley who has returned to us and whom we welcome back to our Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, your Honours, thank you very much. Good afternoon learned counsel. The first witness this afternoon, Mr. President, has sought certain protective measures from the Tribunal. He wishes to have his face and voice distorted. Unfortunately for technical reasons this cannot be done, because there is a technical failure with the voice distortion equipment, so the Prosecutor will be applying on his behalf for a closed session this afternoon, only in respect of that witness. I have spoken to my learned friends on the Defence; they are not in disagreement with using that process; indeed Rule 75 does envisage, a closed session in certain circumstances for the protection of witnesses, so, Mr. President, if you are in agreement with that, we can proceed in that manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: First, I would like to know how long this system is going to be not working, if every single time there are technical problems we run into these same consequences, and this really is not a good thing. I would like to remind you that we are holding public hearings, even if the witnesses have to be protected. Mr. Dubuisson, have you anything to add to that?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, we are aware of the problem and trying to resolve it as quickly as possible, but I cannot tell you how long that is going to take at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We do not oppose, your Honour, a closed session for purposes of basically granting face anonymity, facial anonymity for the witness, but I would assume that the transcript will not need to be sealed, if we use a pseudonym for the witness. At least the parties and the court can cite to the transcript the testimony of this witness in public documents, so we would make that request and I assume it is consistent with the Prosecutor's objectives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think it is obvious that is true, is it not, Mr. Cayley? Since the witness was supposed to have been heard in an open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think the point that my learned friend is making is that he may wish to cite to the transcript, and the only manner in which that can be done is if the witness also has a pseudonym, although, of course, because it is a closed session in any event, his name will not be made public, but the transcript will be, if it is to be referred to, so he will have to be referred to in court under a pseudonym. I agree with that comment, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If he wanted a pseudonym, he would have had to have had a pseudonym in an open session with face and voice distortion anyway, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right then, we can sustain that objection. So the only protective measures that had been asked for were distortion of his face and voice, but he was not trying to have his name held back; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: He does wish to have a pseudonym, Mr. President. Indeed if he had had his face and voice distorted, the image would have been transmitted to the public and he would have had to have been referred to as Witness A, B or C, although in a closed session there will be no public transmission of the proceedings in this courtroom, the point that Mr. Hayman makes is that the transcript is still a public document and thus that will be released to the public, so he will still have to be referred to as Witness A, B, C. It is difficult, I know, but unfortunately it is a result of this technical failure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right, perhaps the technical -- the equipment will help us out. Would you tell everybody what you just told me.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Apparently, if we wait for ten minutes, we can have voice distortion and image as well. For the image there is no problem. The problem was related to the voice distortion. After the witness, we have to wait for about ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right then, we will suspend the hearing for ten minutes in order to make the equipment operational. (2.30 pm) (A short break) (2.50 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We can resume the hearing now. Once again, let us be sure that everything is working right. Mr. Cayley, we will give a pseudonym to the witness. What pseudonym did you choose, Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness T, Mr. President. I would also apply, Mr. President, that the first part of the testimony will be in completely closed session and the last part, because the witness will be speaking of matters which will identify him to the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, we will ask the witness to remain seated. Witness T, you agreed to come to this Tribunal to testify. First we ask you to identify your name, but do not state it. Just look at the piece of paper being shown to you by the usher and then read, while remaining seated, the statement which has been given to you. WITNESS T (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We are not quite sure that the technical equipment is functioning properly. If it is not, we will simply have a closed hearing, but I want to say very clearly, so that we do not have the witness brought back again, if the technical conditions have not been prepared in the future, then either you must not bring in the witness or postpone it for another day, because it is not really dignified for a Tribunal to get up, go out, come back in. Either the technical equipment works or it does not. I understand if it does not, but in that case, we must be advised in advance, and it is not a very good thing for the witness either. In any case, we will begin now with Witness T and I will ask the Prosecutor to summarise for the judges what he expects from the witness. Do you want us to go into a closed session now?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: You are not talking about a private session here?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: A private session; no transmission to the public at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right, private session. (In closed session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (In open session)

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness T, you said that the government worked satisfactorily until or during this time during 1991. I would now like you to move on and explain to the court the negotiations that took place with representatives of the JNA in Zenica as to the departure of JNA units in Busovaca, and what those negotiations ultimately led to in respect of relationships with the HDZ in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I pointed out, the year 1991 was excellent in terms of work. We worked together. The Municipal Assembly gave us very high marks for our work, both the President of the municipality and the President of the Executive Council of the municipality. At that time, problems began in Slovenia and Croatia, the JNA attack on Slovenia and Croatia, and we felt that problems would spread to Busovaca or rather to Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was the time when the representatives of the municipality took action and they elected a Crisis Staff. It was elected by all the parties, the aim being to conduct talks and negotiations with the former JNA, for them to move out of the barracks, and there were two barracks in Busovaca. One was based in Rajlovac and the other one in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness T, was there an agreement with the HVO in Busovaca as to the division of the Territorial Defence in those barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were separate talks, but as a civilian, I did not fully participate in them, but there was talk of the arms being shared half and half, the arms that were in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness T, shared between whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Between the HDZ and the SDA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the division was supposed to occur between the SDA and the HDZ, can you explain what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was happening in 1992, somewhere around April or May, and I think that there were some problems that arose in that connection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As a result of those problems, can you explain to the court what happened in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As a consequence of those problems, on May 9th 1992 a command was issued which was signed by responsible officials of the HVO, or rather Herceg-Bosna, to the effect that all the armaments should be taken over by the HVO, and that night, in the evening at 1.20, rather early in the morning at 1.20, according to the order that you have a copy of, Busovaca was blocked, Croatian flags were hoisted at the police station in Busovaca, as well as at the Municipal Assembly building. The post office was captured. The work of all democratically-elected bodies was banned, as well as all parties, the HDZ and the Executive Council; everything was taken over by the HVO. Actually, I could describe it as a military coup. Furthermore, in all companies, the directors were appointed by decision. They were of Croatian ethnicity, even though there were Bosniaks holding managerial positions in some companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness T, if you could pause there and if the witness could be shown exhibit 208? Mr. President, 208 is an exhibit in BCS. 208A is a French translation of the same document and 208B is an English translation of that document. Witness T, do you recognise this order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do, it is the order which I was handed in the morning by the SDA President at 5.00 am, and that night, Dzemal Merdan and Alija Begic were arrested, and this order was signed by the Vice-President of the HVO, Mr. Dario Kordic, whose signature I am personally familiar with, and the Commander of the municipal staff of the HVO Busovaca, Ivo Brnada, who was an active duty officer in the former JNA. This order was entirely fulfilled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness T, I do not want you to read this order to the court, because everybody can read it. You have mentioned a number of events that took place as a result of it, but what was the general effect after this order was issued in the town of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The general effect was that, as I mentioned earlier, flags were hoisted, a military coup was carried out, the work of all legally-elected bodies was banned, bombs began to be planted in Bosniak-owned businesses, and some were set on fire, among them, the shop owned by Senad Hevacic, by Fadir Dizdarevic, Besad Mehanovic, Emin Saracevic, Faik Sarajlic, and so on and so forth. All shops owned by Bosniaks, and after that Mirsad Delija was killed on his doorstep.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness T, who was responsible for all of these actions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that the people who signed this order were responsible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness T, there was, I believe, a subsequent order of 22nd May, and if the witness can be shown exhibit 2099, and there is again a French and English translation of this order. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By whom is this document signed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This document was signed by the Vice-President of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, Dario Kordic in person, and the President of the municipal HVO staff of Busovaca, Florijan Glavocevic, but there is no need to read the order because it is all written there, all that it contains, and it was acted according to this order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness T, were there Croats in Busovaca who opposed the contents of these two orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I must say that there were decent Croats, honest people, especially local ones, the people who were there for ages and who condemned these steps, and in particular, a doctor, a well known specialist called Franz and his son. He too was earlier a member of the HDZ, and the former Vice-President of the HDZ also opposed this. His name was Dragutin Cicak, who, after several articles that he wrote in the press was beaten up by certain people in Busovaca. They were HVO representatives, and there are reports about this in the press. He was beaten up, even though he used to be the Vice-President of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness T, you have mentioned a number of incidences that occurred, of businesses being blown up, and I do not wish you to repeat yourself, but can you briefly describe to the court the life of the Muslim population in Busovaca between May 1992 and January 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is only logical that the Bosniaks became scared, and, of course, they denounced this. Some of them, for these reasons, started moving out, because they were afraid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness T, on the night of 21st January 1993, you received a call from Florijan Glavocevic. Can you explain to the court the conversation you had with Mr. Glavocevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a good friend with Florijan Glavocevic. We are roughly of the same age. For many years, he was head of the Sumarija, the forestry enterprise in Busovaca. He was in charge of the nursery, forest nursery in Busovaca, and also I had bought a piece of land from his mother. His mother was about 30 metres away from my house. Maybe on 20th or 21st January he called me up on the phone from the Busovaca municipality building, where a session of the HDZ was being held. He asked me secretly to go to his mother's, and indeed in ten minutes' time, I went out and he told me that I should move out as soon as possible. I should leave Busovaca, because an order had come from the Defence minister of Herceg-Bosna, Bozo Rajic, to attack Busovaca, and with my friend who was visiting at my home with his wife about 6.00. His name was Ibro Hodzic, and taking my relative's car, we only just somehow managed to reach Zenica, and we stayed there for a certain period of time, and Ibro Hodzic later -- was later killed in his own apartment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness T, did you try and communicate this warning to anybody else in the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had quite a number of friends, and I wanted to warn them, but I did not succeed, because the telephone lines were cut immediately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you flee to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I fled to Zenica, with my wife and son, and my colleague Ibro Hodzic, with his wife and son, and I am still in Zenica; I am living in somebody else's apartment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think a couple of days after this incident occurred, you returned to the village of Kacuni near Busovaca. Why did you return?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right, I met a colleague of mine, Husnija Neslanovic and Nihad Pasalic and they invited me to go to Kacuni so that we could review the situation as it was in Busovaca at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you discussed, did you not, forming a War Presidency; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was not a War Presidency, it was roughly a kind of Executive Board of the SDA, which reviewed and discussed the situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To look after the interests of the Bosniak people of Busovaca; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Bosniak people, yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you return to your house in Busovaca that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On that day, I went back to my house in Busovaca to protect some things, and leave them with my neighbours, Croats, and my son was with me, and my daughter-in-law, so I wanted to get them out too, to save them. However, I could not get out, because again, everything was under blockade, so that I spent the night at a friend of mine's in a building on the fifth floor, with my son and daughter-in-law. This was on the 24th, it was a Sunday, a Sunday evening, and the next day at 6.00, the sirens could be heard. Heavy fire from all weapons and armaments, especially in the Bosniak areas known as Kadica Strana, and I saw through the window Bosniak houses being set on fire. I saw that the HVO had set light to about five houses, I know exactly whose they are, and after that, another 14 or 15 houses, therefore a total of about 19 houses were torched, all in a line, and I saw this with my own eyes looking out of the window, because this is nearby. I saw HVO soldiers entering the houses and setting them on fire, and them bursting into flames and burning down completely. Later on that same day, I also personally witnessed people being expelled from Kadica Strana, both men, women and children. They were brought in front of the fire brigade centre and I saw men being separated and being taken away to the camp at Kaonik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness T, what was the ethnicity of the men, women and children that you saw being taken to the fire brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were only Bosniaks, only Bosniaks. I spent two nights at my friend's house, and the next day, in the morning at 7.00, they came to fetch me, two HVO soldiers came with the insignia, and they took me away, together with another colleague of mine, to the camp at Kaonik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness T, what did the two HVO soldiers say to you when they came to find you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They told me that they had received orders to arrest me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness T, what had you done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had to go with them, because they were armed with automatic rifles, and I went without making any comments, because I had to go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what was the reason that they arrested you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The reason was that I was a Bosniak, a Muslim, because it was not just me that was arrested. All people who had Bosniak names were arrested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you were taken to the camp at Kaonik. Can you describe to the court your detention in that facility, and the events that took place whilst you were there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It is correct that I was taken to the camp at Kaonik, which was specially built for that purpose. There were some 20 or so cells. I was admitted by Aleksovski, whom I knew personally, and there was another man with him from Zepce. I was admitted and my colleague; we were registered and shoved into cell number 9. These were cells roughly 3 by 3 metres in size. There were 18 of us in there. Let me add that in the camp at the time, there were between 300 and 400 Bosniaks, civilians. I underline the word civilians, and I was one of them. With me was Jasmin Sehovic; he is a young man of 18, a civilian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: May I just ask a question? Witness T, you mentioned that there were 20 cells and 300 civilians. In the 20 cells? How were they packed in 20 cells?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wish to observe that there were not just cells; there were also some larger halls, military halls, therefore in addition to the cells, those who could not fit into the cells went into the halls and for a time I too was moved from the cell to the hall. Two or three times I was taken out there and we would spend the whole night walking up and down. These are concrete halls, concrete, cold, January, and all we did was walk up and down so as to protect ourselves from the cold.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Witness T, just to clarify a couple of points: this prison facility, the HVO were running it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe to the court incidences that took place whilst you were detained at Kaonik, particularly those incidents which occurred at night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Almost every night there were callouts of people. Names of prisoners were called out and they were taken to dig trenches. People were taken to be used as human shields in the capture of certain villages like Skradno, Kovacevac, Loncari and so on. During trench digging, some people were even killed. One of those who was with me in the cell is Sehovic, Jasmin Sehovic, and thus also Mustafa Ibrilic was killed, as well as Nermin Elezovic, because on two occasions, people were taken to the Kaonik camp from the 25th January until 8th February, when an exchange was carried out through the mediation of the International Red Cross, and then again in April, when again a certain number of people were killed on the front-lines. I personally did not see that, I heard about it, I read about it, and we amongst ourselves knew who those people were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness T, you stated that individuals that were detained were used as human shields. Can you explain to the judges what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HVO more or less wanted to take, to capture certain villages which I have mentioned, Skradno, Strane, Loncari, Kovacevac, et cetera. They went head first and they were tied up. They wanted to be protected by them, because their aim was to take the villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "they", you mean prisoners from Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HVO. The prisoners were like human shields.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the HVO, as the HVO advanced on this village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anybody beaten from your cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From my cell, Jasmin Sehovic was killed, because he left the cell and never came back and there were other people who were killed. They were not from my cell but from other cells, Mustafa Ibrilic, Jasmin Elezovic, and then there were other people from the cell who were beaten, they were actually being beaten. There was one man who was with me, his name was Cago. He came from the police, he was in the police force in Busovaca, and he told me that he had been beaten, and I could see this personally. He had -- his ear was cut by a knife, and also he had a scar on his neck and also a cross on his stomach. This was Cago who was with me and who otherwise was a neighbour of mine. Apparently this was done by members of some special police from Mostar, that is from Herceg-Bosna. I do not know the names, but I saw this personally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These were HVO special police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You saw the scars on this man's body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was any property stolen from any of the individuals within your cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From amongst the prisoners, watches, gold rings and money was taken. They were taking anything of value from them, but later on, and this I have to say, during the exchange on 8th February, some of these belongings, some of the watches and the rings were produced and they asked to whom some of these things belonged and to those people who could identify those got them back. Then the exchange took place with the assistance of the International Red Cross. The Red Cross arrived on 5th February, that is four or five days later, and I personally saw salvation for myself and for others in them, otherwise it would not have ended well. It is possible that we would have been killed; that is a possibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness T, when this property was being returned to the prisoners at Kaonik, was there a film crew filming this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The International Red Cross filmed all this, as well as certain local stations, so all this was filmed, and I am sure you have lists from the International Red Cross about who was there. I also received an identity card from the Red Cross, and I received a certificate from Zagreb which you have in the file.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the return of the property to prisoners filmed by the film crew?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Could the witness now be shown exhibits 210 and 211? (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this is mine, this is myself, this is what everybody else also had. If they did not receive this certificate, then they have this from the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were exchanged, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When the exchange took place, I went to Zenica, and a colleague of mine, he was the SDA President, returned to Busovaca because his wife was there, and after the cease-fire and the Washington Agreement, his wife was killed, a bomb was thrown into the house, and he was wounded, one of his legs was shattered and a portion of the other one too, and he is in rehabilitation in Denmark. Also after the cease-fire in Busovaca, the mosque was set on fire, and in all villages where the HVO had control, the mekteps, the mosques were set on fire. All this was documented, all this was taped and it can be seen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness T, how many Muslims remain in the town of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the town of Busovaca, there are 26 Muslims left, for the most part, members of mixed marriages and a few who have been protected by their honest neighbours who are Croats. I know more or less which Bosniaks these are by names. Some of these mixed-marriage couples have since moved to the United States.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: If the transcript could be sealed from this point? These are the final questions, Mr. President. (In closed session)

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: (In open session)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your nationality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bosniak Muslim, otherwise I need to say that we lived together, without any problems. We lived together on excellent terms, until the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Mr. President. If I could apply for admission of the exhibits which is 208, 208A and B, the French and English translations; 209A and B being the French and English translations of the same document, and then 210 and 211, a certificate and identification card relating to this witness in respect of his Red Cross registration in 1993. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We would like to note two things, your Honour. Some of these documents predate the time period of the charges in the indictment, which I think raises some questions that I would quite frankly like to consult with my co-counsel at greater length on before taking a position in that regard. Also I think I would state, we have no objection to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You have or you do not have an objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I think what I am saying is I would like to speak to my co-counsel before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That is your right, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The reason being that some of these documents are outside the period of the charges which raises a question in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I think, Mr. President, I can clarify this for my learned friend immediately. The documents before you, the orders relate to the month of May 1992, and I can direct --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Which document are you speaking about? First, are there any objections about 208 and 209, those two? Let us try to see where we are. 208 and 209, these were the documents identified by the witness. There is no objection about those I suppose. That is the command orders on 10th May 1992 and 22nd May 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: 10th May I think predates the -- no? I can shoot from the hip or I can have a moment, Mr. President, to confer and then we can give you a definitive position. That might be more efficient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You try to offer some clarifications, but obviously Mr. Hayman wants to speak with his colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Do you want us to confer now, Mr. President? I am sorry. Is the court waiting for us to take a position on these exhibits?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, I thought you were going to do it right away. If you need ten minutes, instead of taking our break at 4.30, we can take our break right now, until 4.45. Would you prefer doing it that way?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I am uncomfortable keeping the court waiting. Perhaps after the next break we could advise the court, not to dictate we take a break now necessarily. If it is convenient to take a ten-minute break now, we can do that and advise the court at the end of the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, we are not going to take two breaks. We have already lost a lot of time today. I was thinking we would take our break at 4.30, but since the examination-in-chief has been completed and you wish to confer with your colleague, perhaps with the accused, perhaps a little bit longer than just a few moments, apparently you need some more time, I was suggesting the following solution, that is we take a break right now, say 20 or 30 minutes, and then resume around 4.45, at which point you could tell us what your answer is and we could settle this incident. Does everybody agree to this? Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Very quickly, Mr. President, can I please make one observation? These two documents date from 10th May 1992 and 22nd May 1992. The month of commencement of the second amended indictment is May 1992, therefore it is the position of the Prosecutor that these documents are relevant and admissible. If my learned friend has any further comments to make then we can wait until after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I think it is most efficient that we take the break and we can then advise the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right, we are going to take a 20-minute break and begin at 4.35. (4.15 pm) (A short break) (4.35 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed. Please bring in the accused. (Accused brought in)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, your Honour, for giving us a moment to confer, that is my co-counsel and I. As to exhibits 210 and 211, the ICRC documents, we have no objection. As to exhibits 208 and 209, we have two points. The first is that the documents are not relevant to any charges against our client. The second superseding indictment charges in paragraph 3 that the accused became the Regional Commander of the HVO for the Central Bosnia region on June 27th 1992, so these documents predate his authorities and responsibilities as the Regional Commander. There has been no evidence from this witness that the accused had any personal involvement in any of the events in Busovaca prior to June 27th 1992, and, by definition, the accused, could have no command responsibility for any events in Busovaca prior to June 27th 1992, because he was not a commander with responsibilities that included the Busovaca area prior to 27th June 1992. So we have a relevance objection to the documents. Secondly, exhibits 208 and 209 purport to be Herceg-Bosna or HVO documents. Although we have no particular quarrel with the contents of these documents, in fact we believe they relate to other persons and not to the accused. As a matter of principle, we note that, strictly speaking, the documents have not been authenticated, and so we make an authentication objection to them, unless, of course, the same standards will be applied to Defence documents, in which case we make no such objection. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The first point that I would like to make, your Honours, is that the commencement date of the second amended indictment is the beginning of May 1992. The two documents to which my learned friend refers date from 10th May 1992 and 22nd May 1992. In the prosecution of any criminal offence before any court, it is expected of a Prosecutor to bring background information to set a scene in which criminal offences were committed. This is exactly what these documents do. They chart the commencement of conduct by HVO officials in the Lasva Valley. They demonstrate that the HVO began its plans at an earlier stage than when my learned friend states from the indictment that General Blaskic was appointed to a position within the HVO. The second point that I would make on the date of May 1992 is that the Prosecutor charges persecution beginning on that date. When the Prosecutor speaks of persecution, we do not refer to one instance at one time; we refer to a pattern of conduct which stretched from May 1992 to January 1994, in which we say the defendant, General Blaskic, participated. It matters not that the Defence may state, and I say they may state, that he joined this process at a date later than May 1992; we say it commenced and he was a senior official who participated in that. In respect of the authenticity of the documents, that objection has absolutely no foundation whatsoever. The witness identified the documents. He stated that he had seen them at the time in May 1992, that copies had been placed in front of him, original documents. It is my respectful submission that that clarifies the authenticity of the documents entirely, so it is the Prosecutor's position that these documents are relevant, they should be considered with all of the other evidence that the Prosecutor presents to the court and that their authenticity has been established by this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hayman?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I stand on the record and on my objections, unless the court has any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like to consult with my colleagues. (Pause). The Tribunal will receive as evidence documents 208 and 2099. Furthermore, the judges next week will render the decision on the entire question regarding the admission of documents, specifically as indicated in the brief which was submitted by the Defence several weeks ago. I think we can now move to the cross-examination. Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, I will try to be brief. Good evening, Witness T. The first question is: could you please tell me what percentages did the SDA and the HDZ win in the first elections?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Busovaca had 48 per cent of Croats, 45 per cent of Bosniak Muslims, 6 per cent of Serbs and others. Out of 8,800 inhabitants, about 9,000 were Croats, 8,500 were Bosniaks and 600 Serbs and others. So the HDZ had two more Council men, because there were about six parties, there were the Reformists the SDP and the others, where Bosniaks, Croats and Serbs were all included. So the two winners were the HDZ and the SDA, so there was a coalition. There was no problems, the co-operation was excellent up until a certain period.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said about the military coup on 9th May 1992. What I am interested in is who was in charge of the civilian administration? Was it the civilian authorities or the military wing of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How did you call it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The executive administrative power, that is who was the Executive President of the Council of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Up until the May 1992, it was a civilian government, up until 9th May. That was the day of independence of Croatia. On that day, there was a military coup and after 10th May, it was the HVO, starting 10th May when the order was issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You did not understand the question. Do you distinguish between the military and the civilian structure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the HVO only had the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very well. In those events in May 1992, did anybody in any context mention General Blaskic or Colonel Blaskic at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, at that time Filipovic was mentioned in this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, who formed the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff was established by the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: On whose instructions was this done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was there a co-ordination board for the protection of Muslims in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only later.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How much later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Later, that is after the events that took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The burning of the -- the torching of businesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you place it in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Somewhere around September, maybe August or September, I do not know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What year?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What was the function, or what was the goal of this committee for protection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was to protect Muslims in certain ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Were representatives of the Muslim part of the army and police involved in this board?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You mentioned the meeting of the SDA in Kacuni at which you were present. Was the purpose of this meeting the establishment of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What was the purpose?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was discussion surrounding the issues -- the problems created by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What were the conclusions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were no conclusions. I did not know much about it. I was involved in the civilian matters like delivery of food to the Muslims, because they were under siege.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Who established the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nobody organised the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did the War Presidency in Busovaca exist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Later on it did. It existed -- it was established in February 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Who established it in February 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The SDA gave the proposal to set it up and to provide for food and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You mentioned the order of Bozo Rajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Whom you called the Minister of Defence of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Minister of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you know at that time Bozo Rajic was Minister of Defence for the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the state of whom Alija Izetbegovic was the President; did you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you see the order of Bozo Rajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, Floro Glavocevic told me that this order had been issued to attack the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So Florijan Glavocevic told you that the order was issued to attack the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But in the examination-in-chief when asked by my learned colleague the Prosecutor, you said that the order was given to attack Busovaca. There is a difference there. What is the truth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So the order was to attack the Army of BiH or Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The BH-Army and Busovaca, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What exactly did Florijan tell you, Florijan Glavocevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He told me that the positions of the army had to be attacked, the BH-Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And nothing more?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In whose house are you living now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am living in Zenica, in a house owned by a Serb who has moved out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Are you paying rent to that Serb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not for the present.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Has he sold you that apartment, has he given you permission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never saw him, the house was empty. There was a hospital or rather a pharmacy of the HOS in Zenica there before, HOS, which is an organisation within the framework of the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the HOS in Zenica was within the framework of the BH-Army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was more inclined towards the HDZ, because in that house, I came across -- personally I found a large number of papers indicating HVO Zenica, headquarters Zenica et cetera. I burnt them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You mentioned 19 houses that were burnt; can you tell us exactly where they are?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kadica Strana.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What is the name of the street?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Bosniak side. It is either Redziplavas or Hadzeterica Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know exactly where the front-line was in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, I was not familiar with military things.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You mentioned that your friend had told you that there was an order to arrest Muslims. Who gave the order, did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When did I say that? Can you clarify that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When your friend advised you to flee, that Muslims would be arrested, you said that your friend told you that an order had been received to arrest Muslims, so my question is: did that friend tell you who issued the order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said that the army positions would be attacked and that I should flee, because he was a friend of mine, and he told me to flee with my family and just then, people were being arrested, people were disappearing, people who held responsible positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did an order arrive to attack the BH-Army positions or did the order come regarding the attack and the arrests? What did he say? Which of these two actions were ordered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Therefore the order was to attack the positions of the BH-Army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, you know the President of the municipality Maric?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course I do, we worked together.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did he have to flee from Busovaca as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the coup, the military coup, Maric was removed for about ten or fifteen days. He went to the seaside and as soon as he came back, he resumed his position.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: He is a Croat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In your examination-in-chief, you said that Kaonik was a camp specially built for that purpose?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What was the building before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These were military facilities, but a company called Vatrostalna, with which I worked, by instructions from the HVO had specially built the cells. I personally recorded this. It cost 95,000 German marks, the job done by Vatrostalna.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Were you mistreated in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not. Do you know why I was not? Because I personally knew Aleksovski, and I knew people who were in charge of the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And who were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were people from the HVO police. There was Zarko Petrovic in the police, Zeljko Katava et cetera, but the main one was Aleksovski; he was in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Remember when you were talking about human shields, I would like to know how do you know, who said that people were used as human shields?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: People who came back to my cell, because for about five days, I was in one cell, cell number 9, and in that cell, there were 18 people, and almost all of them were taken to dig trenches and for use as human shields and so on, and then later on, the cells were changed, we were moved to other facilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you give me the name of the person who told you that he was used as a human shield?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Faik Sarajlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Who else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Lusija, and others, I cannot recall, it was a long time ago, but there is no doubt about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that those people were used as human shields in attacks against Loncari, Kovacevac and Skradno, so my question is: was there any resistance put up in Loncari?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Well then how could they be used as human shields if there was no armed resistance from Loncari?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe they thought there were people there, but there were only civilians there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So there was no battle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were more or less civilians. They were intimidating people, houses were being burnt down. Loncari is my village; it has been completely burnt down by the HVO, and some civilians, quite a number of civilians were killed, civilians without putting up any resistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: That is why I am asking, how could they have been used as human shields if there was no resistance in Loncari?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They thought there would be some resistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But there was not any?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They expected it, but there was not any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, the question has already been asked, the answer has been given. He said that he thought they were used as human shields and that is clear. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Skradno, who controlled Skradno?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How could people be used as human shields when Skradno was attacked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were people, but afterwards, the HVO had control, but in Skradno, Skradno is inhabited by Bosniaks, close to Sajtovic, the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was there any resistance in Skradno? Again I am asking you how could they be used as human shields?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They expected it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Kovacevac. Who had Kovacevac under control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now it is the HVO and the village has been totally burned down by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was there any defence in Kovacevac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, I was in the camp at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How could they be used as human shields?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, I would like to remind you that you are dealing with professional judges. We have understood the sense of your question on one of the sites. The answer was given that the HVO legitimately or illegitimately, according to the information you have, might have run into resistance, but you do not go through every single one of these sites with the same answers. Please let us speed things up. Go ahead, move forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. The killing of Sehovic, Elezovic and Mustafa Ibrilic, who told you about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Jasmin Sehovic was with me in the cell. He went to school with my son together and he went from the cell to be used as a human shield to dig trenches and as a human shield and he was killed over there. He did not come back, and the same occurred to Mustafa Ibrilic. I did not see it, but he is not there, he has been killed. There are documents to show this and there are witnesses who may perhaps come here to tell you about it. The same applied to Elezovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I am asking you, who told you under which circumstances those three men were killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because they were Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You have not answered my question. Which person told you under what circumstances those three men were killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have said that this young man, Sehovic, was with me in the cell and he did not come back and I was told, there were 18 of us in a cell 3 by 3, 18 men. We slept like this, (indicating) leaning to the side.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You have not answered my question. Who told you under which circumstances those three men were killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You mentioned Cago. Did somebody try to cut his ear? Where was this done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the police station in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you were registered by the International Red Cross, you went for an exchange. Who were you exchanged for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Where did those people come from? What ethnicity were those people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. I know that we were Bosniaks and that we were exchanged. With whom and how, I do not know. I suppose the International Red Cross knows.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you have the possibility to say, "I do not want to be exchanged; I want to stay." Could you say that to the International Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Who would say that? Who would say such a thing?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I am asking you, did you have such a possibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You mentioned that the mosque in Busovaca was destroyed. When was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know the date, but it was after the signing of the treaty, the Washington treaty.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: That is February 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know the date, but it was after the treaty was signed, but let me add that the mekteps, medzidi in Kovacevac, in Loncari, Skradno were all burned down in all the villages, the places of worship, and there are photographs of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Are you perhaps aware of what the percentage of the area of Busovaca was under the control of the BH-Army and what share was under HVO control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Roughly 60 per cent by the army and 40 per cent by the HVO, but the HVO had the downtown area, all the companies, and the army the surrounding villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you see or hear anything at all about Tihomir Blaskic in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not. Later on I heard about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have two or three more questions but for a closed session, so that the identity of the witness may not be disclosed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is this not a closed session?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We are talking about the transcript, because this part of the transcript will not be revealed to the public at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No objection from the Prosecution? (In closed session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (In open session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: This is in open session. You requested partial protective measures which were granted to you by the Tribunal. What the judges ask you to do is to speak without fear, and to say things that you like. After several questions which the Prosecutor will ask you, who asked you to come to testify before us and you will testify about the events in Busovaca, what you noted about the HVO in relation to yourself, the arrest of your husband, under detention conditions to which he was subjected before being murdered, plunder and possibly Ahmici. You will be guided as you are deposing, when necessary, by the Prosecutor. Perhaps preliminary questions, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not on my point.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you. Good evening, Ms. Sahman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I am going to ask you a series of preliminary questions as we have discussed and then I am going to ask you to give a narrative answer to the judges in respect of the events that occurred to you and your husband. Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If you could keep your voice up, it would be very helpful to the court and to the interpreters as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will try indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Ms. Sahman, are you a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina and a Muslim by faith?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Are you 40 years old?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were you born in the village of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Before the war, did you get married to a man by the name of Fadil?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you then thereafter have two children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Fadil was also of the Muslim faith; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Before the war, was your late husband employed as a bus driver for the Zenica Transport Company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When I say before the war, I am referring to the war between the Muslims and the Croats, so you understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he did work there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Before the war between the Muslims and the Croats, did he join the TO and did he go to Turbe to fight against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I believe you told me he went to the front-lines on one occasion and thereafter he returned to his job as a bus driver at the Zenica transport correct; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you and members of your family live in the Municipality of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at Kaonik in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your home in fact was located next to the Busovaca T-junction; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I could have exhibit 212 shown to the witness and presented to the bench and to counsel and to the witness lastly? Ms. Sahman, I am going to show you a photograph that you and I have talked about before coming into court. Mr. President and your Honours, this exhibit 212 is an enlargement of a portion of a previously entered exhibit, Exhibit 59 and it is accompanied by a legend which is attached to the back. Can you see that exhibit in front of you, Ms. Sahman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: There are three numbers mentioned on this particular exhibit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity to examine with me and then place on this particular exhibit these locations that are indicated as numbers 1, 2 and 3?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 1 is my house, 2 is the village of Strane and 3 is where my husband dug trenches, the house of Vlatko Franc.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The area to the right-hand side of that that says "Kaonik" is the location where your husband was imprisoned by the HVO, Kaonik camp; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is right here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Ms. Sahman, I would like to now ask you to testify about the events that occurred to you and to members of your family in January and February of 1993. Could you please tell the judges what occurred to you and to members of your family at the hands of the HVO, starting in January 1993 and continuing thereafter. Tell the judges, please, Ms. Sahman, in your own words, at your own pace, in a style in which you are comfortable explaining the story to the judges.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 24th in the afternoon about 5.00, I came home from Ahmici and we passed by the checkpoint, because our house is nearby. We parked the car, we went in, we fed the cattle, we went into the house, it was already dark, we looked down, there was no light at the checkpoint. We thought there was no particular reason. We were in the house. My husband liked to play chess and he would play chess with the children. I was doing something else, I do not recall. About 9.30, it was time to go to bed, but we were watching television, when suddenly the bell rang. My husband got up to open the door. He asked, "Who is it?". The answer was, "The HVO police". We immediately jumped up, my husband opened the door, a pistol was pointed at my chest immediately by one man, and two or three others came in with this one. We started screaming, asking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me. You are speaking a little bit too fast. Could you slow down just a bit so the interpreters can do their work properly. Everything is fine; go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will, I will. They came in, pointing their guns at us. My husband was there, we were shouting, "What is wrong?" They said, "You have to surrender your weapons." I and the children started shouting. He did not say anything, he just said, "The weapons I have are those I have had for a long time. They are mine. I have nothing else. But I need to have a receipt from you, a piece of paper to show somebody took it from me, because tomorrow some other people may come to ask for weapons." He said, "You tell them Miro Ljubicic from Kacuni took the weapons and everything will be okay." One of them said, "What are you waiting for? Why do you not start the fire?" The pistol was still pointed at us. It was not an easy situation, and then my husband said, "Here are the rifles, take them", and they took them and they asked, "Who else has weapons?" We said we did not know, this is what we have and then they went. That night we spent talking about what was happening, but my husband was bold and strong and he just tried to calm us down. He did not say anything more. Of course I and the children were a little more scared than he was. Then the next day at 6.00, the sirens could be heard and we knew the sound when there was the alarm for general danger. Then either the brickworks or Vatrostalna, one of the two factories, I do not know which one it was, we thought something bad was about to happen, but we were surrounded and there was nowhere that we could go, and when they took the weapons from us, there were about 20 of them down there. There was a large group of them, so we saw that we did not have a chance to go anywhere. After that, the shooting started in the direction of the village of Strane. It was very heavy fighting, almost to what we heard before when the army was there, where the camp is now. The bullets did not hit our house while we were there, and for two days it went on like that, and then I could smell smoke from burning, but we kept quiet for two days, and after that, five or six times the HVO police kept coming, demanding weapons. We said we had given them in and then they said, "You have sniper" and we said, "We do not have any." Then three or four of them would come and take my husband out behind the house. They would talk, I do not know what about, and they kept saying, "Surrender the sniper", and we said, "But we do not have", because we really did not have a sniper; our neighbours know that. Then they said, "We were given orders you had a sniper", so we shrugged our shoulders, because we did not know what they meant. This went on for five or six days, and then one day my brother-in-law came and said, "Up there in our village they are reporting on the radio that there is a sniper shooting from behind Sahman's house", and we said we did not know what it was about, so my husband took the car and went to the village and he came across Ivica Andrijasevic there and they all got into the car and went into the cafe-bar, restaurant called Sunce, and my husband said, "I do not know what they want of me." He said, "Let us go to your house and look around; maybe somebody does have a sniper there." So they came, they walked around, they did not find anything, so they said, "You go into your house and no one will touch you." Then my husband said, "That is what they told me, but things are not good." Whatever the situation, we had nowhere to go, considering the position of our house. Then one day they came to take our car. They asked us, "Do you have a car?" We said, "Yes". They said, "We need it." Close to my house was my brother-in-law's house and there was an alarm fitted to it and one of them went to break in, one downstairs, two upstairs. One of them shot at the alarm. We could hear the shooting, we were just watching, and that is how it was, and then my husband went to fetch the car, and they told him, "Do not switch it off." This was only five or six metres away. We could see everything from the terrace. My husband got out, they got in, my son started crying and my husband told him, "Never mind, we will buy another one." We went back into the house and then Dragan Vujica came, because he had heard the shooting. To this day, you can see the holes from the sniper bullets, and then he asked, "What is happening, neighbour?" My husband said, "They took my car." He said, "If you need anything, I am here." My husband, when he gave them the car, he went to his brother's house and when he came back, he said that all the furniture had been turned over, these were just a few minutes, they did not have time to take anything with them. They did not, but then others came back, wearing uniform. There were various types taking things. Then they came to our house, asking for the TV set, the video-recorder and we said, "Here you are, take them." Then Goran and someone else from Jajce came and we had to play tapes which we did not want to listen to, because we felt embarrassed that people with weapons could come into the house and sit with us, but my husband said, "You just keep quiet", and then he asked them, "Would you like anything?" We had meat and drinks and we wanted to offer them something, and they said, "No, we just want tapes. Let us see what tapes you have. This one, that one; play this one, that one." So it went on. Then the next day or the day after, they came for the video-recorder and the TV set and then we hoped they would not bother us so much again. They came five or six times during the daytime and at night to insist with my husband to give up the sniper and he kept saying, "But I do not have one. Ask my neighbours, those I went hunting with. They are Croats and Muslims and Serbs and they will tell you that I never had a sniper." But they kept insisting. What they said to him I do not know, but when they came into the house, they would say, "I do not know why you keep insisting; why do you not give it up?" I said, "I do not have it". I thought to myself that if I could find it, I would get it and give it to them, just to get rid of them. And so it went on like that for quite some time. Then on 4th February, they took him to the camp. They came early in the morning about 8.00. My husband went out and they took him behind the house and the other two came in, and they asked, "What do you have?" We said, "nothing". Then my husband came back and said he had to go immediately and I said, "Why are you bothering him? What do you want of him?" He said he had to go. Before that, we had divided the money we had among the children and my husband and each one of us had a little in case something would happen and so he took the money with him to the camp as well as his watch, and when he -- and so he was taken somewhere, I do not know where. We stayed behind and we wondered what we would do all alone there, with no one. Then they did not come as often. Every couple of days a group would come by looking for something, asking us how we were, and we would say we were okay. Then when my husband went to the camp, for a time they came looking for my son who was 15 years old and they said they needed him, and I said, "Do not take him", but they did not do anything in particular, they did not bother me too much. They let me alone. Then one day, a young man came and asked, "Is this Sahman's house?" I said, "Yes", and he said, "Sahman has sent me to get us some food and bring it to us. We are at the house of Vlatko Samac, we are working there", so I said, "I dare not go there, I am afraid. There is food, but I do not know what to do." So he said, "All right". I do not know what he told them, and there was an empty area in front of our house towards Franz's house. I saw they were working there, doing something, I do not know what, and then I saw my husband there with his arms behind his back, a man behind him with a machine-gun, a short gun. I suppose it is a machine-gun, I do not really know, and then my husband came and he said, "I have come to take that stuff, because the food is very bad. It is very salty, the bread is stale. It is in my pocket but I cannot eat it and I know that we have plenty of food, so we can give some to other people too." When he started off -- he came into the house, he just said, "It is not good", and walked up and down. This man insisted that he should go. This all lasted a minute or two, and when my husband saw the bag, he said, "No we cannot take that now", so my husband took a piece of cake that we had on the table. It was the size of a large apple perhaps, and he took that and held it behind his back as he did his arms, and he went off with this man following him in camouflage uniform, with a chequer board sign on his cap and the HVO insignia on his sleeve. We stayed behind. We would have liked to go somewhere, but we did not know where or what to do. After dark, a young man came. My husband sent him again. He comes from the Simica Kuce, because we know him, our brother-in-law painted his house, so he was among those who worked there and he said to me, "I do not know what is happening." He just shrugged his shoulders, so he took what he did and went off; I assume they got it. Then on 8th February, we heard that they were going to be released from prison, and my husband wanted to go to the other area, some people were going to Zenica. They asked Sahman, "Where do you want to go?" He said "I do not know." Some people went to Zenica, some to Vitez and he said, "I do not know where or what to do." They asked, "Where is your family?", and he said, "At home." They told him, "You must go home too because they will be mistreated if you leave." He said, "Okay, I will go home", so he came and there were other neighbours from the village coming. We had quite a lot of cigarettes, we had alcohol and drinks. My husband did not drink, but he had some for the guests and he said, "I will give you something to drink." Some people came in, others just dropped by. He gave them cigarettes and I do not know what else and they left and we stayed behind. He said things were not good, but there you are. He said, "I was not well. I was in small premises and it was very hot. I thought my heart would break. I asked to be taken to the doctor's, but they would not and they said, 'If you are hot, why do you not go over here?' It was another premise, another room. This was long and big and I froze there", he said, so I did not know which was better the one where it was hot or the one where it was cold. "Luckily I did not spend much time there, only four nights, whereas the others...", and I said, "Well, what can we do, as long as we are alive?" Then he said, "I went to work near Franz's house, and the others were taken further away. There was a blue van with the HVO signs, the chequer board sign. We did not see the licence plates or anything else. We saw our car, the licence plates had been removed. They probably did not have time to attach others with the HVO insignia." We spent those days there. It was not easy. We did not know what to do, nor could we do anything, so the days went by, and my husband complained. I asked him where his watch was, and he said, "Never mind the watch", and I said, "What about the money? You had quite a bit", and he said, "Never mind the money; we will get money somehow, some day." So that is all he said, "Never mind the watch, never mind the money", and so we went on. He said, "I was quite lucky", but he was complaining of his back. Whether he was hit or not, I did not see any signs of blows or maybe he had a cold or something, but something was wrong, because he complained. Time went by, until 13th February, and that morning, we decided to send our children to Loncari, because he said, "We cannot go on like this", so he said, "You children go to Loncari and we will follow, but we do not know when." That morning the children got ready. I have a sister-in-law up there, they got dressed, and he said, "How beautiful my children are", and I said, "They are not beautiful." I saw that he was moved by something. The children left, we stayed behind. Then we had the cattle and he said that he did not know what to do. He kept repeating, "It is not good, it is not good", and then if I felt bad, he would say, "Things will get better." Then the children reached Loncari, and we thought if there was someone to go with them, they could go to Zenica too, but anyway that night they did not go. We sat in the house, my husband and I. The TV was on because we had a couple of TV sets, the children had a computer, we had three TV sets to be precise. They took away the colour TVs, but we had a black and white one. We were watching this programme, "Image on Image". I said, "Are there any good news?", and he said, "No, they are not good news." Those were the words he used. We had a dog outside and I heard him barking. I wanted to say, "This is not good", but I did not dare, I did not want to bother him, and then the bell rang, somebody rang hard. He was a strong man, he jumped up and opened the door. Whenever anyone knocked, we would jump up immediately, that was our habit from before. He opened the door, and when he opened it, I saw a gun under the left arm. He said, "Get out." My husband kept quiet, he never uttered a word. He repeated, "Get out", and I said, "Where are you taking him?" My husband said, "Let me get dressed", and he said, "There is no need", and I again said, "Where are you taking him?" Then my husband put his hand through my hair and they were forcing him out. One of them was very big. He had a chequer board sign on the cap. He had two big moles, at least they appeared to be big to me. This other one was shorter. He turned around to put on his slippers and they said, "There is no need. Get out."
