I kept saying, "Where are you taking him?", and then the third man followed. This was about 6.30. It was already evening, and near the garage there were lots of them. I did not count them, but there were plenty in camouflage uniforms. "What are you doing to him? What has come over you?" Then one of them said, "Turn it off", so I did not know what he meant. What am I supposed to turn off? Then I went outside through the corridor and I could hear shots. I went to the terrace again. I cried out, I shouted, there was not a soul left, so I thought to myself, "What in heaven's name is happening?" I came back. We had a telephone, but they would cut the lines often, so that we could not communicate with other towns, but we were able to make local calls, and since Dragan Vujica came by one day and said, "If there is anything you need, call me", so I picked up the phone and I called him up, Dragan Vujica. His wife answered and she said, "Dragan is not here." "I need him", I said, and she said, "Call later." So then I called his father, Mirko, and I told Mirko, "They have taken my husband. Could you come with me somewhere? I do not know where, but I called you for help", and he said, "I cannot come", so I said "All right." I went out of the house. Passing by the sheds and my neighbour Cama was there and I said, "They have taken my Fadil. I do not know where, I do not know what to do." So we spent the night in a small apartment, we did not even dare stay in her house. I was there for maybe an hour. I did not have a watch, and then I said, "I am going to look around. Maybe he is wounded or something, so I want to look for him. If not, I may go up to the village of Strane"; that is what I told her. She would not let me go, but I still insisted and I set off. I went through the yards, but I could not -- I just turned around and went back. It was dark, it was so dark. It was never so dark, or that was my impression. So we spent that night and then the next day we got up and we went again by the sheds and stables and we reached my house. I looked around and there is no Fadil nowhere to be seen. Then the steps were there leading outside, and I was still looking around, and then I said to her, "You go up front, because..." Then she said, "There he is", and I followed her. She went on to the village of Strane; I stayed there. He was lying there on his stomach, his hands were crouching, he was bleeding, not then, but before. He was wearing white socks, blue sweatsuit and coloured T-shirt. I started screaming, I cried and then UNPROFOR came by. I waved, they saw me, but nothing. When the HVO shift went by to Strane. They passed by our house and we could see them from the window, from everywhere. That morning, they went from the direction of the Vujica houses that morning, and they saw me. They could see me from up there, I assume they could see me, but nothing. They did nothing, so I kept on crying, walking up and down. They went by, they paid no attention and then my brother-in-law arrived, and he said, "I do not know what happened", and I said, "You see what they did?" We stood there and, of course, he cried too, it was his brother, and that is how it was. Then he said, "I should go and ask someone what we should do." So I said, "All right, you go." Then another neighbour, an elderly man, came to stay with me. He left, I do not know who was the person responsible for this. He came back shortly and he said they would allow ten men to bury him and nothing more than that. I said, "But he is a Muslim? One dies only once; we need to perform the religious rites." He said, "We do not have the ability." So I said, "Very well, what can I do?" Then the men came, all elderly people. They carried him into the house. Four or five of them went to dig the grave, and then I again mentioned the need for a Hodza. He deserved a Hodza, but they said there was nothing they could do. So we carried out the burial. It was not easy, it cannot be easy. No one can understand who has not gone through the same experience. By then darkness fell, the men came into the house, there were some women preparing food. I said, "There is plenty of everything. Prepare food for them, let them eat their fill", so they did and the men came and ate and I said, "Why do you not all stay here with me?" They said, "We dare not", so I said, "In that case I will go with you", so I went with them up there. We spent the night. He had a mother and a father. His father died afterwards and then in the morning, my father-in-law said, "What about the cow and the other animals?" I said, "We left them behind", so we agreed to go down there and feed them, and when we got there, somebody had already broken into the house. "Let them be, let them take whatever they want", I thought to myself, "they have done the worst. The fact they are looting is the least of our problems." That is what my father-in-law also said, he agreed, but it was not easy for him, for any parent to lose a child, and he was born in 1911. Whenever we came, we saw something new. He went to his other son's house, and he said they had looted everything, but I tried to console him. I said, "We have no rights here. What is what they want and they can take what they want." That is how it went on for two or three days. I sat there and I said to myself, "I will go to the infirmary", where we used to have an infirmary. I wanted to seek protection from them, and a woman came by and I said, "Let us go there", and we went and when we got there, we found somebody called Maric from Podolje. There are several brothers. I do not know all their first names, but it is easy to find out. I said to them, "I have come to ask for protection, because I see what you are doing. I cannot leave the house, but look what you have done to me, so let me have what is left and I would like some protection." He said, "You go to your house and no one will do any harm", so I went back home. They said nobody would harm me and yet you see what they did to me. So we sat there and a neighbour of mine, an elderly man, his wife was away visiting, so he spent some time with us, then his own house, then in his daughter-in-law's house. He himself did not know what to do. Then I saw somebody coming up the steps and I recognised the man. His name was Ivica Sendula. He was with two twins, Simic, and they were with a large dog. They were wearing uniforms, there was a chequer board on the cap and the HVO insignia on the sleeves, but I knew him. He was a colleague of my husband and I knew him well, so I did not mind. He had a notebook, and he said, "I am sorry, neighbour, but I have to register the population, the number of households and members of households", so I said, "Very well." Then he pointed to my brother-in-law's house and he was abroad, and he said, "How many of them are there?" I said, "There are four of them, husband and wife, and they have two children." He asked for their names. I gave the names, the names of my brother-in-law and his wife, but I just could not remember the children's names. Then I said, "The boy's name is Paul, there are two sons, they are boys", that was all I could remember. Then he heard that somebody else was there, and I said, "It is only my neighbour". He said, "I need his name too", because he was making lists of all the houses, so the neighbour came out and he reported himself and his wife's, and then they left. We asked ourselves what it was all about, and that was how we spent that time, up and down. I could not stand it any more alone, the children had left. I wondered whether they had heard what had happened to their father or not, so I just could not stay any more, and then I set off. I decided to go to Ahmici to my family, and I left everything, because you have to think of yourself too. You see you have to go, you do not know where, so I went there, I spent a night there, and I was wondering what had happened to my children. I should go to Zenica, I thought to myself, and then my relative said, "We have already been to visit our children in Zenica." They said, "We heard from our neighbours, Croats, that Fadil has been killed, that he had a sniper, that he had a radio transmitter and I do not know what else, but we said what he had and everyone knew that." Then I got ready and went off to Zenica. I stayed with my niece for a month and a half. Then they found an apartment for us, a colleague gave us this apartment and that is where I stayed with my children. When we got there, there was nothing, everything was empty. My son sat there, he had nothing. Then I tried to console him, "Never mind, my son, everything will be all right." Then God helped us, we had friends, and they collected all kinds of things for us, so we survived, we collected what was essential, so, of course, it was not fine, it can never be fine again. Never can we have what we had once, and so I stayed there with my children. When April 16th came, that morning, I was sleeping in Zenica and dreaming shells falling on Ahmici. I cried out, I screamed and I told the children, "There are shells on Ahmici", and they said, "No mother, it cannot be." I said, "You will see, they are doing whatever they want." So we had this debate amongst ourselves, we had a telephone. I said, "Call them", and then I approached the phone. I called up my father, brother, one brother, another brother, a third brother. No one answered, so I thought to myself, "What can it be?" So I was half crazy by then. I called two nephews who were living further away, neither of them answered, so I kept crying out, "What can it be?" Then I brought my neighbour from across the way, his name is Adem, and I said to Adem, "I am calling my family and no one is answering, what is happening over there?" He said, "Our houses are burning, my wife has been wounded, I do not know what it is all about." So I hung up and I said, "Take care." On 16th April, I could not do anything, I could not call anyone, but on the next day I called Ivica Cerkez and I got him on the line. His house borders on our fields and he could see people coming in and out of the house and I introduced myself. I said, "My name is Smaila, Ivica, I am calling to see what is happening, I cannot find my people." He said, "The houses are not all right but I do not know what has happened to them." I said, "But what is happening, Ivica?" He said, "It is the war." I said, "Very well, let it be", so I hung up, I cried out, I cried, I did not know what to do. This went on for two or three days. One of my sister-in-laws called.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Ms. Sahman, let me ask you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, we listened to this and all the intensity that we heard in her voice. Perhaps she is a bit tired now. I think this would be a good time to end the hearing for today. I think she has almost finished. I am sure you will have some questions you want to ask her, some clarifications about certain points which she may not have completely explained. You will not have her repeat what she has already said. You will have to come back tomorrow. We will start at 2.15 and we hope that you spend a restful evening. We will now suspend the hearing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. (6.35 pm)
